arbitrary

AR-bih-trair-ee — ends like 'very scary'; arbitrary rules feel scary because there's no reason behind them. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Arbitrary is based on random choice or personal whim rather than any reason or system.

The coach's decision to bench the team's best player seemed completely arbitrary.

Example

On the first day of class, the teacher made the arbitrary choice to assign seats by pulling names out of a hat. Students asked why they couldn't sit alphabetically or choose their own spots. The teacher shrugged and said there was no particular reason.

Arbitrary describes a choice made with no reasoned system behind it. Unlike 'unfair,' which implies someone is harmed, an arbitrary decision may hurt no one — it simply lacks any justification.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

random: Random means happening without any pattern or plan at all — a coin flip, a lottery draw. An arbitrary decision is different: someone deliberately chooses, but with no reason or system behind the choice. Random has no chooser; arbitrary has a chooser who cannot justify the pick.

capricious: Capricious means driven by sudden, unpredictable whims — eager one moment, dismissive the next. Arbitrary points at the decision itself: made without reason or system. A capricious ruler keeps changing course on impulse; an arbitrary rule may never change at all and still rest on no justification.

whimsical: Whimsical means guided by playful impulse rather than logic, and it usually sounds charming — a whimsical garden, a whimsical story. Arbitrary is a criticism: a choice with no reason behind it. Whimsical suggests lighthearted fancy; arbitrary suggests an unjustified and often resented decision.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

reasoned: based on careful logic

systematic: following a fixed, orderly plan

Where it sits · how little reason lies behind it — offhand → arbitrary → tyrannical

offhand vs. arbitrary: An offhand choice is made quickly and casually but may still have some sense behind it, making it weaker than arbitrary, which means there is no reason at all.

tyrannical vs. arbitrary: A tyrannical rule is stronger than an arbitrary one — it is not only reasonless but also cruel and oppressive.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — arbitr-

root — arbitr-: judge (Latin)

suffix — -ary

suffix — -ary: relating to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin 'arbiter' meant a judge who decided matters at his own discretion. Something 'relating to the judge's discretion' came to mean decided by one person's whim alone rather than by fixed rules.
